rule: Decree 63-457, still identified by the official trade portal as the governing instrument, requires an import permit before ordering covered goods (article 2). Article 1(b) expressly covers any dried plant; article 5 applies articles 1 and 2 to every import whatever its size. The current portal also requires a sanitary or analysis certificate for processed plant-origin products. Applying the broad dried-plant provision to identifiable dried sencha leaves is an interpretation of the statutory wording, not a tea-specific written ruling.
personalMailApplicability: Article 5 expressly extends the permit provisions to all imports regardless of size, with baggage mentioned as an additional example rather than an exclusive route. A 100 g personal parcel therefore does not obtain a small-quantity exemption under this text.
quantityLimit: No small-quantity exemption: article 5 applies regardless of import size.
authority: Côte d’Ivoire official trade portal; Decree 63-457 of 7 November 1963, official gazette scan held by FAOLEX
researchAttempts: Read the chapter 09 agricultural import workflow and searched personal-use, noncommercial and postal exceptions.

Read the actual official-gazette text of Decree 63-457, especially articles 1(b), 2, 5 and 6; cross-checked continued use against the current official PWIC page. Located the primary FAOLEX scan through its exact ECOLEX record. Read Law 64-490 and Order 509/2014 via the German NPPO mirror; did not treat generic commercial tax thresholds as agricultural exemptions.
permitFreeReason: The current official portal relies on Decree 63-457. Articles 1(b), 2 and 5 together impose prior permission on dried plants irrespective of shipment size. Application to dried sencha leaves is an inference from that express scope; the required prior permit conflicts with the store’s no-permits policy. This is not a claim that tea is prohibited.

rule: The official 2023 MINADER legal compendium confirms the manufactured-product pest-risk definition and that Decree 2005/0771 article 3 reserves import licences for high-risk products identified by ministerial order. Its 2019 inspection-fee annex explicitly names tea leaves and manufactured products, and separately covers postal/courier platforms; the fee schedule does not itself determine whether sealed steamed sencha requires a foreign certificate or prior licence.
personalMailApplicability: Postal/courier and accompanied-baggage inspections are expressly contemplated. Neither the inspected fee schedule nor the implementing decree establishes a certificate-free route for 100 g manufactured Japanese tea.
authority: Cameroon NPPO laws filed with IPPC
remainingQuestion: Does the applicable high-risk/regulated-product determination cover manufactured steamed sencha, and does the personal postal route require a foreign phytosanitary certificate or special application?

Searched the ministerial/NPPO high-risk commodity list and tea-specific determinations. Excluded an inspection fee listing as conclusive evidence of an import certificate requirement.
permitFreeReason: No no-document route verified. Current official consolidated rules distinguish high-risk licence requirements from inspections, and tea appears in the inspection fee schedule. That evidence is insufficient either to exempt the parcel or to assert that all manufactured tea necessarily needs a licence/certificate.

rule: The NPPO’s published PR01-23 import-permit procedure requires an application, risk analysis and origin phytosanitary or disinsection certification for goods within its plant/plant-product scope. It expressly cites ISPM/NIMP 5 and 32. Neither it nor Law L/92/027 assigns manufactured steamed tea to a risk category; the law limits manufactured-product coverage by pest risk.
personalMailApplicability: No tea-specific personal postal allowance located.
authority: Guinea NPPO law filed with IPPC

Read the complete two-page national procedure PR01-23, including its risk-analysis step, origin documentation and references to NIMP 5/32. Checked the government services portal and agriculture procedures index. No tea-specific category or personal-post waiver located.
permitFreeReason: The current national permit procedure is verified, but its application to manufactured sencha remains unresolved because the underlying product definition is risk-based. Referencing NIMP 32 is not by itself a national tea exemption.

rule: Law 17-004/AU of 2017 imposes permission/certification requirements for regulated plant goods, including post, with manufactured products defined by pest risk. Food Law 17-005/AU expressly includes personal-use food (article 6(I)(g)), but its examined certificate provisions concern specific animal products and import businesses; it does not resolve a certificate requirement for plain manufactured tea.
personalMailApplicability: Post is expressly covered under Plant Law article 59 when goods are regulated. Food Law article 6 includes personal use, so private consumption cannot be treated as a blanket exemption from food rules; manufactured-tea classification remains unsettled.

permitFreeReason: Neither a blanket personal-use exemption nor a tea-specific certificate requirement is established. The plant-law risk qualification remains decisive. The later food law includes personal use but does not by itself impose the examined animal-product certificate rules on tea.
